prompt: Write an email to your manager, Priya, declining her invitation to a planning meeting on Friday at 4 p.m., because you will be at a client site in Leeds that afternoon. Propose two alternative times on Monday. Include a subject line and keep the email under 120 words.
rubric: Has a subject line that names the meeting and the request to reschedule. Declines the Friday 4 p.m. meeting clearly and politely, with the reason (at a client site in Leeds). Proposes two specific times on Monday. Tone suits a manager: respectful and concise, without over-apologizing. Ends with a clear next step, such as asking which time works. Under 120 words.

prompt: Write an email to a customer, Mr. Alvarez, whose standing desk (order #58213) will arrive 9 days later than promised because a supplier shipped a faulty part. Apologize, explain briefly, and offer him a choice: a 15% refund on the desk if he keeps the order, or free cancellation with a full refund. Tell him how to let you know his choice.
rubric: Apologizes sincerely without groveling. States the 9-day delay and the reason (a faulty part from a supplier) briefly and honestly, and mentions order #58213. Presents both options clearly: a 15% refund if he keeps the order, or free cancellation with a full refund. Explains exactly how he can reply with his choice. Warm, professional tone. Does not invent policies, dates or compensation beyond the brief.

prompt: Write a firm but polite email to your landlord, Ms. Carter, asking her to repair the heating in your flat. It has not worked since 3 November, you reported it by phone on 4 November, and nothing has happened since. Ask for a repair date within three working days.
rubric: Clear subject line. States the problem and the key dates (not working since 3 November, reported by phone on 4 November) and that there has been no response. Explains the practical impact briefly. Asks clearly for a repair date within three working days. Firm and polite: neither hostile nor vague, no threats. Proper greeting and sign-off.

prompt: Write a product description of 100 to 150 words for the Quietline noise-cancelling headphones, aimed at university students. Use these facts: 40-hour battery life, folds flat for a backpack, a transparency mode for hearing announcements, weighs 220 grams, costs $129.
rubric: Uses all five facts accurately (40-hour battery, folds flat, transparency mode for announcements, 220 g, $129) and invents no other specifications. Connects the features to student life (library, lectures, commuting, long days). Vivid but not exaggerated. Ends with a call to action or the price. 100 to 150 words.

prompt: Write an app store description for Tiny Steps, a habit-tracking app for busy parents. Include a one-line hook, three key features as bullet points, and a closing call to action. Keep it under 150 words.
rubric: A strong one-line hook aimed at busy parents. Exactly three concrete features as bullet points, each framed as a benefit for parents with little time. A closing call to action. Friendly, encouraging tone without exaggerated health or productivity claims. Under 150 words.

prompt: Write a 60 to 90 word product description for a refillable stainless steel cleaning spray bottle that is sold with concentrate tablets. The audience is eco-conscious renters. Mention that one tablet makes 500 ml of cleaner and that a pack of 10 tablets costs $12.
rubric: States both facts accurately (one tablet makes 500 ml; 10 tablets cost $12). Speaks to eco-conscious renters: less plastic waste, little storage space needed, easy to use. Clear and persuasive, with no invented claims such as certifications or test results. 60 to 90 words.

prompt: Write a short story of 250 to 350 words about a lighthouse keeper who receives a letter addressed to someone who died 40 years ago. End with a twist that is surprising but makes sense.
rubric: A vivid setting and a believable keeper. The letter drives the plot. The ending twist is surprising yet prepared by earlier details, so it feels earned on rereading. Clear beginning, middle and end. Fresh, specific language rather than clichés. 250 to 350 words.

prompt: Write a bedtime story of 150 to 250 words for a five-year-old about a small robot who is afraid of the dark. Use simple words and end on a calm, reassuring note.
rubric: Simple words and short sentences suited to a five-year-old. A gentle problem (the robot's fear of the dark) resolved with kindness or a comforting discovery. Nothing frightening or overstimulating. Warm, playful tone and a calm ending that suits bedtime. 150 to 250 words.

prompt: Write a piece of flash fiction, under 200 words, in the second person ("you"), about someone who misses the last train home.
rubric: Written consistently in the second person. Under 200 words. A clear moment of tension and some change or realization. Concrete sensory details. An ending that resonates. Avoids clichés.

prompt: Write an internal email announcing that the office is moving to 25 Canal Street on Monday 2 March. Staff must pack their desks into the boxes provided by 5 p.m. on Thursday 26 February, label each box with their name and floor number, and work from home on Friday 27 February while the movers work.
rubric: Clear subject line. States the new address (25 Canal Street) and the move date (Monday 2 March). Lists the actions and deadlines accurately and in an easy-to-scan way: pack desks into the provided boxes by 5 p.m. on Thursday 26 February, label each box with name and floor number, work from home on Friday 27 February. Friendly, positive tone. Says where to send questions. Invents no logistics that contradict the brief.
